claim: The small RNA Qrr1 is a regulatory component of the quorum-sensing system in V. fischeri.
source: Previous work has shown that the small RNA Qrr1, which is a regulatory component of the quorum-sensing system in V. fischeri, promotes host colonization.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as background information.

claim: Qrr1 promotes host colonization in V. fischeri.
source: Previous work has shown that the small RNA Qrr1, which is a regulatory component of the quorum-sensing system in V. fischeri, promotes host colonization.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as background information from previous work.

claim: Transcriptional activation of Qrr1 is inhibited by the sensor kinase BinK.
source: Here, we report that transcriptional activation of Qrr1 is inhibited by the sensor kinase BinK, which suppresses cellular aggregation by V. fischeri prior to light organ entry.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract.

claim: BinK suppresses cellular aggregation by V. fischeri prior to light organ entry.
source: Here, we report that transcriptional activation of Qrr1 is inhibited by the sensor kinase BinK, which suppresses cellular aggregation by V. fischeri prior to light organ entry.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as part of the findings.

claim: Qrr1 expression depends on the alternative sigma factor σ54.
source: We show that Qrr1 expression depends on the alternative sigma factor σ54 and the transcription factors LuxO and SypG, which function similar to an OR logic gate, thereby ensuring Qrr1 is expressed during colonization.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Qrr1 expression depends on the transcription factor LuxO.
source: We show that Qrr1 expression depends on the alternative sigma factor σ54 and the transcription factors LuxO and SypG, which function similar to an OR logic gate, thereby ensuring Qrr1 is expressed during colonization.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Qrr1 expression depends on the transcription factor SypG.
source: We show that Qrr1 expression depends on the alternative sigma factor σ54 and the transcription factors LuxO and SypG, which function similar to an OR logic gate, thereby ensuring Qrr1 is expressed during colonization.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract.

claim: LuxO and SypG function similar to an OR logic gate in regulating Qrr1 expression.
source: We show that Qrr1 expression depends on the alternative sigma factor σ54 and the transcription factors LuxO and SypG, which function similar to an OR logic gate, thereby ensuring Qrr1 is expressed during colonization.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract.

claim: The regulatory mechanism involving LuxO and SypG is widespread throughout the Vibrionaceae family.
source: Finally, we provide evidence that this regulatory mechanism is widespread throughout the Vibrionaceae family.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Coordination between the signaling pathways underlying aggregation and quorum-sensing promotes host colonization.
source: Together, our work reveals how coordination between the signaling pathways underlying aggregation and quorum-sensing promotes host colonization, which provides insight into how integration among signaling systems facilitates complex processes in bacteria.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: V. fischeri is a bioluminescent bacterium.
source: The bioluminescent bacterium Vibrio fischeri (also known as Aliivibrio fischeri) is a notable example of a bacterium that depends on multiple signaling systems to establish and maintain association with a host (Miyashiro and Ruby, 2012; Verma and Miyashiro, 2013; Visick et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction.

claim: V. fischeri depends on multiple signaling systems to establish and maintain association with a host.
source: The bioluminescent bacterium Vibrio fischeri (also known as Aliivibrio fischeri) is a notable example of a bacterium that depends on multiple signaling systems to establish and maintain association with a host (Miyashiro and Ruby, 2012; Verma and Miyashiro, 2013; Visick et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The Hawaiian bobtail squid Euprymna scolopes is the best characterized host for V. fischeri.
source: While a variety of marine animals serve as hosts for V. fischeri, the Hawaiian bobtail squid Euprymna scolopes is by far the best characterized, and this host–microbe association has emerged as a powerful system to model how signaling systems function in a natural host environment.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction.

claim: V. fischeri populations emit bioluminescence from a specialized light organ located within the ventral side of the mantle of E. scolopes.
source: From a specialized light organ located within the ventral side of the mantle, populations of V. fischeri emit bioluminescence that camouflage the host when viewed from below (Jones and Nishiguchi, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Bioluminescence emitted by V. fischeri camouflages the host squid when viewed from below.
source: From a specialized light organ located within the ventral side of the mantle, populations of V. fischeri emit bioluminescence that camouflage the host when viewed from below (Jones and Nishiguchi, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: V. fischeri grows on host-derived compounds within the light organ.
source: Because V. fischeri grows on host-derived compounds within the light organ (Graf and Ruby, 1998; Wasilko et al., 2019), the association is considered a mutualistic symbiosis, in which each taxon benefits from their long-term and intimate interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The association between V. fischeri and E. scolopes is considered a mutualistic symbiosis.
source: Because V. fischeri grows on host-derived compounds within the light organ (Graf and Ruby, 1998; Wasilko et al., 2019), the association is considered a mutualistic symbiosis, in which each taxon benefits from their long-term and intimate interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The symbiosis is initially established after juvenile squid are exposed to seawater containing V. fischeri cells.
source: The symbiosis is initially established after juvenile squid are exposed to seawater containing V. fischeri cells (Lee and Ruby, 1994), which enables bacterial mutants to be assessed for their ability to establish symbiosis, that is, to colonize, grow, and produce bioluminescence within the light organ.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The light-producing luciferase enzyme is encoded within the lux operon.
source: The light-producing luciferase enzyme is encoded within the lux operon, which is transcribed when signaling by the LuxI/LuxR quorum-sensing system occurs (Miyashiro and Ruby, 2012; Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The lux operon is transcribed when signaling by the LuxI/LuxR quorum-sensing system occurs.
source: The light-producing luciferase enzyme is encoded within the lux operon, which is transcribed when signaling by the LuxI/LuxR quorum-sensing system occurs (Miyashiro and Ruby, 2012; Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Mutants for LuxI fail to produce bioluminescence in vivo.
source: Mutants for either LuxI (autoinducer synthase) or LuxR (autoinducer receptor) fail to produce bioluminescence in vivo (Visick et al., 2000; Yount et al., 2022), which illustrates the significance of quorum sensing for the symbiosis to be established.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Mutants for LuxR fail to produce bioluminescence in vivo.
source: Mutants for either LuxI (autoinducer synthase) or LuxR (autoinducer receptor) fail to produce bioluminescence in vivo (Visick et al., 2000; Yount et al., 2022), which illustrates the significance of quorum sensing for the symbiosis to be established.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Under conditions of low autoinducer concentrations, AinR or LuxPQ can trigger a phosphorelay that results in phosphorylation of the transcription factor LuxO.
source: Under conditions of low autoinducer concentrations, either AinR or LuxPQ can trigger a phosphorelay that results in phosphorylation of the transcription factor LuxO (Miyashiro et al., 2010; Kimbrough and Stabb, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: LuxO activates the transcription of the small quorum regulatory RNA Qrr1 in conjunction with the alternative sigma factor σ54.
source: In conjunction with the alternative sigma factor σ54, LuxO activates the transcription of the small quorum regulatory RNA Qrr1 (Miyashiro et al., 2010; Kimbrough and Stabb, 2015), which lowers the ability of V. fischeri to enhance bioluminescence production (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Qrr1 lowers the ability of V. fischeri to enhance bioluminescence production.
source: In conjunction with the alternative sigma factor σ54, LuxO activates the transcription of the small quorum regulatory RNA Qrr1 (Miyashiro et al., 2010; Kimbrough and Stabb, 2015), which lowers the ability of V. fischeri to enhance bioluminescence production (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: A Δqrr1 mutant can establish a light organ symbiosis with bacterial abundance and bioluminescence emission levels that are indistinguishable from the wild-type strain.
source: For instance, a Δqrr1 mutant can establish a light organ symbiosis with bacterial abundance and bioluminescence emission levels that are indistinguishable from squid colonized with the wild-type strain (Miyashiro et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: When juvenile squid are exposed to an inoculum evenly mixed with Δqrr1 mutant and wild-type strains, they later feature light organs containing threefold fewer Δqrr1 cells than wild-type cells.
source: However, when juvenile squid are exposed to an inoculum evenly mixed with Δqrr1 mutant and wild-type strains, they later feature light organs containing threefold fewer Δqrr1 cells than wild-type cells (Miyashiro et al., 2010), which suggests that the expression of Qrr1 provides an advantage for V. fischeri to establish symbiosis when other potential founder cells are also present.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The expression of Qrr1 provides an advantage for V. fischeri to establish symbiosis when other potential founder cells are also present.
source: However, when juvenile squid are exposed to an inoculum evenly mixed with Δqrr1 mutant and wild-type strains, they later feature light organs containing threefold fewer Δqrr1 cells than wild-type cells (Miyashiro et al., 2010), which suggests that the expression of Qrr1 provides an advantage for V. fischeri to establish symbiosis when other potential founder cells are also present.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: LuxO is a Group I bacterial enhancer binding protein (bEBP).
source: The primary structure of LuxO features an N-terminal regulatory domain, a central catalytic domain, and a C-terminal DNA-binding domain that define this transcription factor as a Group I bacterial enhancer binding protein (bEBP) (Bush and Dixon, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: bEBPs bind upstream of σ54-dependent promoters and hydrolyze ATP to induce conformational changes within the RNA polymerase/σ54/promoter complex that facilitate transcription initiation.
source: As extensively reviewed elsewhere (Bush and Dixon, 2012; Gao et al., 2020), bEBPs bind upstream of σ54-dependent promoters and hydrolyze ATP to induce the conformational changes within the RNA polymerase/σ54/promoter complex that facilitate transcription initiation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The ATPase activity of LuxO is controlled by its N-terminal regulatory domain.
source: Mechanistic studies in other Vibrionaceae have shown that the ATPase activity of LuxO is controlled by its N-terminal regulatory domain (Boyaci et al., 2016), which consists of a REC domain that participates in a phosphorelay (Freeman and Bassler, 1999a; Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In its unphosphorylated form, LuxO is inactive, with a 20-residue linker that connects the regulatory and catalytic domains occupying the active site within the catalytic domain to block nucleotide binding.
source: In its unphosphorylated form, LuxO is inactive, with a 20-residue linker that connects the regulatory and catalytic domains occupying the active site within the catalytic domain to block nucleotide binding (Boyaci et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The linker is a structural feature reportedly unique to LuxO.
source: The linker is a structural feature reportedly unique to LuxO, and its position within the active site is stabilized by hydrogen bonds with the regulatory and catalytic domains (Boyaci et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Substitution of V114 with either alanine or glycine results in a variant of LuxO with elevated activity.
source: This linker model is also supported for the LuxO homolog of V. fischeri—V114 is a residue within the regulatory domain that is predicted to interact with the linker region, and its substitution with either alanine or glycine results in a variant of LuxO with elevated activity (Kimbrough and Stabb, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Phosphorylation of D55 in the LuxO homolog of V. fischeri is predicted to displace the linker.
source: Phosphorylation of an aspartate conserved among REC domains (D55 in the LuxO homolog of V. fischeri) is predicted to displace the linker (Freeman and Bassler, 1999b), which enables activation of LuxO and transcriptional initiation of the qrr1 promoter (Pqrr1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Phosphorylation of LuxO occurs when the histidine kinases that serve as quorum-sensing receptors are unbound with ligand.
source: Phosphorylation of LuxO occurs when the histidine kinases that serve as quorum-sensing receptors are unbound with ligand (Kimbrough and Stabb, 2013; Figure 1); consequently, conditions of low cell density result in LuxO activity and transcriptional activation of Pqrr1 (Miyashiro et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Conditions of low cell density result in LuxO activity and transcriptional activation of Pqrr1.
source: Phosphorylation of LuxO occurs when the histidine kinases that serve as quorum-sensing receptors are unbound with ligand (Kimbrough and Stabb, 2013; Figure 1); consequently, conditions of low cell density result in LuxO activity and transcriptional activation of Pqrr1 (Miyashiro et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Prior to entering the light organ, bacterial cells are collected from the environment and form aggregates that are densely packed.
source: For instance, prior to entering the light organ, bacterial cells are collected from the environment and form aggregates that are densely packed (Visick et al., 2021; Nawroth et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The ΔbinK mutant exhibited 3.7-fold higher levels of GFP fluorescence relative to WT when grown on solid medium to high cell density.
source: When grown on solid medium to high cell density, the ΔbinK mutant exhibited 3.7-fold higher levels of GFP fluorescence relative to WT (Figure 2B), which suggests that Pqrr1 is transcriptionally active in cells lacking BinK.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the results section with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Conditions of high cell density fail to lower Qrr1 expression in cells lacking BinK.
source: Together, these data suggest that conditions of high cell density fail to lower Qrr1 expression in cells lacking BinK.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on experimental data.

claim: BinK inhibits biofilm formation in V. fischeri.
source: BinK is hypothesized to inhibit biofilm formation by either directly or indirectly dephosphorylating SypG to lower transcriptional activation of the syp locus (Brooks and Mandel, 2016; Ludvik et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: The ΔbinK mutant produces wild-type levels of bioluminescence.
source: The ΔbinK mutant produces wild-type levels of bioluminescence, including when the bioluminescence emission per cell unit (specific luminescence) amplifies during exponential growth (Figure 2D), which seemingly suggests that BinK has no impact on how quorum sensing regulates bioluminescence production.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: The specific bioluminescence profile of the ΔbinK rscS* mutant featured a lower peak and lower amplification compared to the rscS* mutant.
source: The specific bioluminescence profile of the ΔbinK rscS* mutant featured an even lower peak and lower amplification (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which suggests that RscS overexpression reveals the ability of BinK to inhibit bioluminescence production.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: RscS overexpression reveals the ability of BinK to inhibit bioluminescence production.
source: The specific bioluminescence profile of the ΔbinK rscS* mutant featured an even lower peak and lower amplification (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which suggests that RscS overexpression reveals the ability of BinK to inhibit bioluminescence production.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on experimental data.

claim: Cells lacking BinK form large aggregates prior to light organ entry.
source: BinK inhibits the aggregation that occurs among environmental V. fischeri cells collected by the light organ, such that cells lacking BinK form large aggregates prior to light organ entry (Brooks and Mandel, 2016; Ludvik et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: Animals exposed to an inoculum mixed evenly with a ΔbinK mutant and its wild-type parental strain result in approximately fourfold more ΔbinK cells than wild-type cells within their light organs.
source: In addition, animals exposed to an inoculum mixed evenly with a ΔbinK mutant and its wild-type parental strain result in approximately fourfold more ΔbinK cells than wild-type cells within their light organs (Brooks and Mandel, 2016), which suggests that BinK inhibits the ability of a cell to establish symbiosis in the context of other colonizing bacteria.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Squid exposed to an inoculum mixed evenly with a Δqrr1 mutant and its wild-type parental strain lead to threefold fewer Δqrr1 cells than wild-type cells within colonized animals.
source: In contrast, Qrr1 provides an advantage to V. fischeri when establishing symbiosis in the presence of other cells, as squid exposed to an inoculum mixed evenly with a Δqrr1 mutant and its wild-type parental strain lead to threefold fewer Δqrr1 cells than wild-type cells within colonized animals (Miyashiro et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Few crypt spaces harbored the Δqrr1 mutant, suggesting that the majority of populations were founded by wild-type cells.
source: Few crypt spaces harbored the Δqrr1 mutant (Figure 3B, C), which suggests that the majority of populations were founded by wild-type cells.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section with reference to Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: The competitive defect of the Δqrr1 mutant is due to fewer crypt spaces being initially accessed by the mutant.
source: Consequently, these results suggest that the competitive defect of the Δqrr1 mutant reported previously is due to fewer crypt spaces being initially accessed by the mutant.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on experimental data.

claim: The ΔbinK mutant occupied most of the crypt spaces following co-inoculation with the wild-type competitor strain.
source: Following co-inoculation with the wild-type competitor strain, the ΔbinK mutant occupied most of the crypt spaces (Figure 3D), which suggests that ΔbinK cells founded more populations than competitor cells and explains the previous observation of higher relative abundance of ΔbinK cells in squid co-inoculated with those strain types (Brooks and Mandel, 2016).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: The ΔbinK Δqrr1 mutant occupied a minority of crypt spaces.
source: The ΔbinK Δqrr1 mutant occupied a minority of crypt spaces (Figure 3E), which suggests that Qrr1 also promotes the ability of the ΔbinK mutant to access crypt spaces.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section with reference to Figure 3E.

claim: Qrr1 promotes the ability of the ΔbinK mutant to access crypt spaces.
source: The ΔbinK Δqrr1 mutant occupied a minority of crypt spaces (Figure 3E), which suggests that Qrr1 also promotes the ability of the ΔbinK mutant to access crypt spaces.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on experimental data.

claim: Most of the aggregates formed by the ΔbinKΔqrr1 mutant were large, suggesting that the impact of Qrr1 on aggregation formation is minimal.
source: Most of the aggregates formed by the ΔbinKΔqrr1 mutant were also large (Figure 3F), which suggests that the impact of Qrr1 on aggregation formation is minimal.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section with reference to Figure 3F.

claim: The Δqrr1 allele is epistatic to the ΔbinK allele during symbiosis establishment.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the Δqrr1 allele is epistatic to the ΔbinK allele during symbiosis establishment, which provides evidence that Qrr1 affects the ability of V. fischeri to enter a crypt space after the aggregation phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on experimental data.

claim: Qrr1 affects the ability of V. fischeri to enter a crypt space after the aggregation phase.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the Δqrr1 allele is epistatic to the ΔbinK allele during symbiosis establishment, which provides evidence that Qrr1 affects the ability of V. fischeri to enter a crypt space after the aggregation phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on experimental data.

claim: The promoter region of qrr1 in V. fischeri features nucleotides corresponding to the canonical −24 and −12 sites (TGGCA-N7-TGC) that facilitate binding by the alternative sigma factor σ54.
source: As with the qrr genes in other Vibrionaceae members (Lenz et al., 2004), the promoter region of qrr1 in V. fischeri (Figure 4A) features nucleotides corresponding to the canonical −24 and −12 sites (TGGCA-N7-TGC) that facilitate binding by the alternative sigma factor σ54 (Bush and Dixon, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations and reference to Figure 4A.

claim: The activity of Pqrr1 of ΔbinK cells depends on σ54.
source: GFP levels in the double mutant were attenuated and comparable to the low levels of the ΔrpoN single mutant (Figure 4B), which indicates that the activity of Pqrr1 of ΔbinK cells depends on σ54.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: LuxO is only partially responsible for σ54-dependent Pqrr1 activity in the ΔbinK mutant.
source: While the GFP fluorescence level of a ΔluxO ΔbinK mutant was lower than that of the ΔbinK mutant (Figure 4C), it was consistently higher than that of the wild-type strain, suggesting that LuxO is only partially responsible for σ54-dependent Pqrr1 activity in the ΔbinK mutant.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: SypG promotes LuxO-independent Pqrr1 activity in cells lacking binK.
source: GFP fluorescence was lower in the triple mutant relative to the ΔbinK ΔluxO mutant (Figure 4D), which suggests that SypG promotes LuxO-independent Pqrr1 activity in cells lacking binK.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: LuxO is the primary activator of Pqrr1 in the ΔbinK mutant.
source: Notably, Pqrr1 activity remained high in a ΔbinK ΔsypG double mutant (Figure 4D), which suggests that LuxO is the primary activator of Pqrr1 in the ΔbinK mutant.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on experimental data with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: Transcriptional expression of the syp locus depends on SypG and is elevated in the ΔbinK mutant.
source: Previous studies have shown that transcriptional expression of the syp locus depends on SypG and is elevated in the ΔbinK mutant (Brooks and Mandel, 2016; Ludvik et al., 2021; Hussa et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: The transcriptional activities of PsypA and PsypP depend on SypG but not LuxO in the ΔbinK background.
source: Both promoters show elevated activity in the ΔbinK and ΔbinK ΔluxO mutants but background levels in the ΔbinK ΔsypG mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), which is consistent with their expression in the ΔbinK background depending on SypG but not LuxO.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Phosphorylated LuxO does not promote transcription of the syp locus.
source: Using a mutant that expresses the phosphomimetic variant LuxO(D55E), we also found that the transcriptional activities of PsypA and PsypP remain inactive in cells with elevated LuxO activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), which suggests that phosphorylated LuxO does not promote transcription of the syp locus.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: While the syp genes are insulated from LuxO, qrr1 can be activated by both SypG and LuxO.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that while the syp genes are insulated from LuxO, qrr1 can be activated by both SypG and LuxO.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on experimental data.

claim: Cells encoding the active SypG variant sypG(D53E) express high Pqrr1 transcriptional activity.
source: Cells encoding this active SypG variant express high Pqrr1 transcriptional activity (Figure 4E), which suggests that phosphorylated SypG leads to Qrr1 expression.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: Phosphorylated SypG leads to Qrr1 expression.
source: Cells encoding this active SypG variant express high Pqrr1 transcriptional activity (Figure 4E), which suggests that phosphorylated SypG leads to Qrr1 expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on experimental data with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: A ΔbinK sypG(D53E) mutant showed higher levels of Pqrr1 activity than either of the corresponding single mutants.
source: A ΔbinK sypG(D53E) mutant showed higher levels of Pqrr1 activity than either of the corresponding single mutants (Figure 4E), which suggests that BinK inhibits activation of factors other than SypG (e.g., LuxO).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: BinK inhibits activation of factors other than SypG (e.g., LuxO).
source: A ΔbinK sypG(D53E) mutant showed higher levels of Pqrr1 activity than either of the corresponding single mutants (Figure 4E), which suggests that BinK inhibits activation of factors other than SypG (e.g., LuxO).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on experimental data with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: Induction of sypG expression was sufficient to activate Pqrr1 transcription in cells that encode BinK.
source: Using a ΔluxO ΔsypG mutant to eliminate background signal to Pqrr1 activity, we found that induction of sypG expression was sufficient to activate Pqrr1 transcription (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section with reference to Figure 4F.

claim: SypG is a bEBP that activates Pqrr1 in addition to the syp locus in V. fischeri.
source: Taken together, we conclude that SypG is a bEBP that activates Pqrr1 in addition to the syp locus in V. fischeri.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on experimental data.

claim: Overexpression of RscS results in wrinkled colonies with elevated GFP fluorescence.
source: As expected, overexpression of RscS resulted in wrinkled colonies with elevated GFP fluorescence (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: The presence of C8 HSL did not alter the wrinkling phenotype and failed to lower GFP fluorescence in cells overexpressing RscS.
source: However, the presence of C8 HSL did not alter the wrinkling phenotype and failed to lower GFP fluorescence, which suggests that Pqrr1 activity remained elevated in those spots.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section.

claim: SypG-dependent activation of Pqrr1 is insensitive to autoinducer.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that SypG-dependent activation of Pqrr1 is insensitive to autoinducer and furthermore indicate a mechanism by which V. fischeri can express Qrr1 even when cells conduct quorum sensing.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on experimental data.

claim: V. fischeri can express Qrr1 even when cells conduct quorum sensing.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that SypG-dependent activation of Pqrr1 is insensitive to autoinducer and furthermore indicate a mechanism by which V. fischeri can express Qrr1 even when cells conduct quorum sensing.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on experimental data.

claim: Two regions within Pqrr1 contribute to SypG-dependent activation: one between −175 and −106 bp and a second between −106 and −60 bp.
source: From these measurements, we found two regions that contribute to SypG-dependent activation, one between −175 and −106 bp and a second between −106 and −60 bp (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: Within each region of Pqrr1, a sequence similar to the TTCTCANNNTGMDWN motif previously reported as the UAS of SypG (UASSypG) was identified.
source: Within each region, we identified a sequence similar to the TTCTCANNNTGMDWN motif previously reported as the UAS of SypG (UASSypG) (Ray et al., 2013), with nucleotides in bold being the only mismatches.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Each site within Pqrr1 features perfect matches of the 13 bp motif TTGCAWWWTGCAA that corresponds to the UAS of LuxO (UASLuxO) reported in other Vibrionaceae members.
source: Notably, each site also features perfect matches of the 13 bp motif TTGCAWWWTGCAA that corresponds to the UAS of LuxO (UASLuxO) reported in other Vibrionaceae members (Lenz et al., 2004; Svenningsen et al., 2008; Figure 6A), which raises the possibility that SypG and LuxO have overlapping UAS within each region.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations and reference to Figure 6A.

claim: SypG and LuxO have overlapping UAS within each region of Pqrr1.
source: Notably, each site also features perfect matches of the 13 bp motif TTGCAWWWTGCAA that corresponds to the UAS of LuxO (UASLuxO) reported in other Vibrionaceae members (Lenz et al., 2004; Svenningsen et al., 2008; Figure 6A), which raises the possibility that SypG and LuxO have overlapping UAS within each region.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the results section based on experimental data.

claim: Substitution of cytosine or adenine within the first half of UASLuxO-2 (C−130A and A−129C, respectively) attenuated both LuxO- and SypG-dependent regulation of Pqrr1 activity.
source: Substitution of either cytosine or adenine within the first half of UASLuxO-2 (C−130A and A−129C, respectively) attenuated both LuxO- and SypG-dependent regulation of Pqrr1 activity (Figure 6C, D), which suggests that these nucleotides are important for both bEBPs to promote Qrr1 expression.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section with reference to Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: Substitution of the guanine (G−131T) had little impact on LuxO-dependent expression of Pqrr1 but decreased SypG-dependent expression.
source: In contrast, substitution of the guanine (G−131T) had little impact on LuxO-dependent expression of Pqrr1 (Figure 6C) but decreased SypG-dependent expression (Figure 6D), which suggests this nucleotide plays a role in specifically mediating how SypG interacts with Pqrr1.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section with reference to Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: The G−131T nucleotide plays a role in specifically mediating how SypG interacts with Pqrr1.
source: In contrast, substitution of the guanine (G−131T) had little impact on LuxO-dependent expression of Pqrr1 (Figure 6C) but decreased SypG-dependent expression (Figure 6D), which suggests this nucleotide plays a role in specifically mediating how SypG interacts with Pqrr1.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on experimental data with reference to Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: A mutant containing the single SypG-relevant G−131T substitution upstream of Pqrr1 resulted in fewer crypts being colonized.
source: However, a mutant containing the single SypG-relevant G−131T substitution upstream of Pqrr1 resulted in fewer crypts being colonized (Figure 6H), which suggests that the ability of SypG to activate expression of Qrr1 is important for V. fischeri to access crypt spaces when competitor symbionts are present.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section with reference to Figure 6H.

claim: V. fischeri is a member of the Fischeri clade of Vibrionaceae.
source: V. fischeri is a member of the Fischeri clade of Vibrionaceae, which includes five species that reside in seawater habitats as well as within squid and fish (Sawabe et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The genomes of representative Fischeri taxa encode homologs of Qrr1 and LuxO on Chromosome 1.
source: The genomes of representative Fischeri taxa encode homologs of Qrr1 and LuxO on Chromosome 1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Table 1) and SypG on Chromosome 2 (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Table 1.

claim: The genomes of representative Fischeri taxa encode SypG on Chromosome 2.
source: The genomes of representative Fischeri taxa encode homologs of Qrr1 and LuxO on Chromosome 1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Table 1) and SypG on Chromosome 2 (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Table 1.

claim: Gene synteny associated with each locus across taxa suggests that the genes encoding Qrr1 and the bEBPs were passed vertically within the Fischeri lineage.
source: Gene synteny associated with each locus across taxa suggests that the genes encoding Qrr1 and the bEBPs were passed vertically within the Fischeri lineage (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claim: For each taxon in the Fischeri clade, alignment of the primary structures for the LuxO and SypG homologs revealed approximately 48% identity.
source: For each taxon, alignment of the primary structures for the LuxO and SypG homologs revealed approximately 48% identity (Table 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Table 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Among the five taxa in the Fischeri clade, 44.4% (214/481) of residue positions in LuxO were identical to the corresponding SypG homolog.
source: Among the five taxa, 44.4% (214/481) of residue positions in LuxO were identical to the corresponding SypG homolog (Figure 7A, B and Figure 7—figure supplement 4), which suggests that the functions associated with various domains of LuxO, including the regulatory linker and HTH domains, are also highly conserved in SypG.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 7A, 7B, and Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: The functions associated with various domains of LuxO, including the regulatory linker and HTH domains, are highly conserved in SypG.
source: Among the five taxa, 44.4% (214/481) of residue positions in LuxO were identical to the corresponding SypG homolog (Figure 7A, B and Figure 7—figure supplement 4), which suggests that the functions associated with various domains of LuxO, including the regulatory linker and HTH domains, are also highly conserved in SypG.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: SypG-dependent expression of Qrr sRNAs is conserved throughout the Fischeri clade.
source: Together, these analyses based on bioinformatics suggest the possibility that SypG-dependent expression of Qrr sRNAs is conserved throughout the Fischeri clade.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: All clades except Rumioensis feature taxa encoding a LuxO homolog.
source: All clades except Rumioensis feature taxa encoding a LuxO homolog (Table 2), with the corresponding luxO gene located on Chromosome 1 in the 17 taxa for which fully assembled genomes are available.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Table 2.

claim: A putative Qrr is encoded in opposite orientation of luxO in 20 of the 21 representative taxa that encode a LuxO homolog.
source: In addition, a putative Qrr is also encoded in opposite orientation of luxO in 20 of the 21 representative taxa that encode a LuxO homolog (Figure 7—figure supplement 6), which suggests that the LuxO–Qrr regulatory system is highly conserved among Vibrionaceae members.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 6.

claim: The LuxO–Qrr regulatory system is highly conserved among Vibrionaceae members.
source: In addition, a putative Qrr is also encoded in opposite orientation of luxO in 20 of the 21 representative taxa that encode a LuxO homolog (Figure 7—figure supplement 6), which suggests that the LuxO–Qrr regulatory system is highly conserved among Vibrionaceae members.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: Among the 21 taxa that encode a LuxO homolog, 12 of them also encode a SypG homolog.
source: Among the 21 taxa that encode a LuxO homolog, 12 of them also encode a SypG homolog (Table 2), and the corresponding sypG gene resides within a gene cluster that resembles the syp locus of V. fischeri.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Table 2.

claim: Most taxa of other SypG-positive clades within the Vibrionaceae that have complete genomes encode the syp locus on Chromosome 1.
source: However, in contrast to the Fischeri clade, most taxa of other SypG-positive clades within the Vibrionaceae that have complete genomes encode the syp locus on Chromosome 1 (Table 2), which suggests the possibility that the syp locus was acquired by a progenitor of the Fischeri clade that arose after diversification from other Vibrionaceae lineages.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Table 2.

claim: The syp locus was acquired by a progenitor of the Fischeri clade that arose after diversification from other Vibrionaceae lineages.
source: However, in contrast to the Fischeri clade, most taxa of other SypG-positive clades within the Vibrionaceae that have complete genomes encode the syp locus on Chromosome 1 (Table 2), which suggests the possibility that the syp locus was acquired by a progenitor of the Fischeri clade that arose after diversification from other Vibrionaceae lineages.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the results section based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: The SypG homologs encoded by non-Fischeri taxa exhibit high amino acid sequence identity to the corresponding LuxO homologues.
source: Despite this possibility of independent acquisition events, the SypG homologs encoded by non-Fischeri taxa also exhibit high amino acid sequence identity to the corresponding LuxO homologues (Table 2), including the same structural features involved in regulating activity (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Table 2 and Figure 7C.

claim: Taxa that encode both SypG and LuxO have the potential for SypG-dependent activation of Qrr sRNAs.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that while the Vibrionaceae lineage has undergone significant diversification with SypG, those taxa that encode both SypG and LuxO have the potential for SypG-dependent activation of Qrr sRNAs.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: Induction of sypGAS expression led to increased GFP fluorescence in V. fischeri ΔluxO ΔsypG mutant harboring a Pqrr1AS-gfp reporter.
source: Using a GFP reporter for the promoter of qrr1AS (Pqrr1AS), we found that induction of sypGAS expression led to increased GFP fluorescence (Figure 8), which suggests that SypGAS can activate transcription of Pqrr1AS and provides support that SypG-dependent expression of Qrr sRNAs can occur in other taxa within the Vibrionaceae family.
evidence: This is a finding reported in the results section with reference to Figure 8.

claim: SypGAS can activate transcription of Pqrr1AS.
source: Using a GFP reporter for the promoter of qrr1AS (Pqrr1AS), we found that induction of sypGAS expression led to increased GFP fluorescence (Figure 8), which suggests that SypGAS can activate transcription of Pqrr1AS and provides support that SypG-dependent expression of Qrr sRNAs can occur in other taxa within the Vibrionaceae family.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on experimental data with reference to Figure 8.

claim: SypG-dependent expression of Qrr sRNAs can occur in other taxa within the Vibrionaceae family.
source: Using a GFP reporter for the promoter of qrr1AS (Pqrr1AS), we found that induction of sypGAS expression led to increased GFP fluorescence (Figure 8), which suggests that SypGAS can activate transcription of Pqrr1AS and provides support that SypG-dependent expression of Qrr sRNAs can occur in other taxa within the Vibrionaceae family.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on experimental data with reference to Figure 8.

claim: V. fischeri has evolved to activate Qrr1 expression by either LuxO or SypG.
source: Specifically, the bEBP SypG activates σ54-dependent transcription of qrr1 in a manner that is independent of its primary bEBP LuxO. Transcriptional activation of Pqrr1 by SypG utilizes two UASs that overlap those sequences associated with LuxO-dependent activation. Together these findings reveal that V. fischeri has evolved to activate Qrr1 expression by either LuxO or SypG.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion section.

claim: The ability of SypG to activate σ54-dependent transcription of Pqrr1 in the presence of high autoinducer levels enables V. fischeri to bypass quorum sensing as a way to modulate the traits regulated by Qrr1.
source: The ability of SypG to activate σ54-dependent transcription of Pqrr1 in the presence of high autoinducer levels is significant because this regulatory link enables V. fischeri to bypass quorum sensing as a way to modulate the traits regulated by Qrr1.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion section.

claim: SypG activates σ54-dependent transcription of the syp locus, which enables V. fischeri to secrete polysaccharides that form an extracellular matrix.
source: SypG activates σ54-dependent transcription of the syp locus, which enables V. fischeri to secrete polysaccharides that form an extracellular matrix (Hussa et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Production of extracellular polysaccharides is necessary for V. fischeri to form the cellular aggregates on the surface of the light organ while initiating symbiosis.
source: Production of extracellular polysaccharides is necessary for V. fischeri to form the cellular aggregates on the surface of the light organ while initiating symbiosis (Yip et al., 2005; Yip et al., 2006; Ray et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Syp-dependent biofilm formation depends on SypG activating expression of all four operons within the syp locus.
source: In culture, syp-dependent biofilm formation, which has been used to model the aggregation observed in vivo, depends on SypG activating expression of all four operons within the syp locus (Ray et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The activation of qrr1 does not appear to contribute to biofilm formation.
source: While this study implicates qrr1 as a member of the SypG regulon, its activation does not appear to contribute to biofilm formation (Figure 5B), which suggests that the Δqrr1 mutant can form aggregates prior to establishing symbiosis, in contrast to mutants containing deletions in other SypG-dependent genes.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: Regulation by Qrr1 enhances the ability of V. fischeri to access a crypt space.
source: However, a Δqrr1 mutant shows fewer crypt populations relative to wild-type cells (Figures 3 and 6), which suggests that regulation by Qrr1 enhances the ability of V. fischeri to access a crypt space.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with reference to Figures 3 and 6.

claim: Environmental V. fischeri cells collected by the squid host express Qrr1 via SypG while forming syp-dependent aggregates along the light organ surface.
source: Taken together, these findings support a model by which the environmental V. fischeri cells collected by the squid host express Qrr1 via SypG while forming syp-dependent aggregates along the light organ surface (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a model proposed in the discussion section with reference to Figure 9B.

claim: SypG-dependent activation of Qrr1 would prime cells to express certain traits that are enhanced by this sRNA, for example, cellular motility, precisely when the transition from the aggregate stage to light organ entry occurs.
source: SypG-dependent activation of Qrr1 would prime cells to express certain traits that are enhanced by this sRNA, for example, cellular motility, precisely when the transition from the aggregate stage to light organ entry occurs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion section.

claim: The ability of SypG to activate transcription of Pqrr1 makes the phosphorylation state of LuxO, and by extension, the corresponding quorum-sensing signaling pathway, irrelevant for expressing Qrr1 during the critical stage of initiating symbiosis.
source: Notably, the ability of SypG to activate transcription of Pqrr1 makes the phosphorylation state of LuxO, and by extension, the corresponding quorum-sensing signaling pathway, irrelevant for expressing Qrr1 during this critical stage of initiating symbiosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion section.

claim: Qrr1 can be expressed under conditions of high cell density through the overexpression of SypK.
source: Interestingly, previous work has demonstrated that Qrr1 can be expressed under conditions of high cell density through the overexpression of SypK (Miyashiro et al., 2014), which is a putative oligosaccharide encoded by the syp locus.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: SypK activates Pqrr1 transcription by stimulating the LuxP/Q complex to trigger LuxO activity.
source: The current model is that SypK, which is predicted to localize to the inner membrane, activates Pqrr1 transcription by stimulating the LuxP/Q complex to trigger LuxO activity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a current model.

claim: A small molecule produced within RscS-induced wrinkled colonies promotes bioluminescence production.
source: More recently, it was also shown that a small molecule produced within RscS-induced wrinkled colonies promotes bioluminescence production (Zink et al., 2021), which suggests V. fischeri may feature additional connections between aggregation and quorum-sensing pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: V. fischeri may feature additional connections between aggregation and quorum-sensing pathways.
source: More recently, it was also shown that a small molecule produced within RscS-induced wrinkled colonies promotes bioluminescence production (Zink et al., 2021), which suggests V. fischeri may feature additional connections between aggregation and quorum-sensing pathways.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion section based on cited work.

claim: Conditions that activate the syp locus lead to the expression of Qrr1 as a mechanism to prime cells for host colonization.
source: The finding that SypG can also activate Pqrr1 further expands the hypothesis that conditions that activate the syp locus, for example, when V. fischeri is initiating symbiosis, lead to the expression of Qrr1 as a mechanism to prime cells for host colonization.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion section.

claim: Homologs of LuxO and Qrrs are encoded by most Vibrionaceae genomes.
source: Homologs of LuxO and Qrrs are encoded by most Vibrionaceae genomes, which underscores their biological significance in regulating the traits associated with quorum sensing.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section.

claim: Over half of the Vibrionaceae clades feature taxa that encode SypG homologs with a high degree of amino acid identity/similarity to the corresponding LuxO homologs.

evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with reference to Table 2 and Figure 7.

source: Such high similarity among primary structures is likely to promote higher-order structures within SypG that function similar to those of LuxO.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the discussion section.

claim: SypG represents the only other bEBP aside from LuxO predicted to contain the regulatory linker.
source: To our knowledge, SypG represents the only other bEBP aside from LuxO predicted to contain this regulatory linker.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section.

claim: The SypG homologs of V. splendidus and V. mediterranei are likely to exhibit constitutive activity or feature other adaptations that accommodate for the altered linker structure.

claim: The signaling pathway that controls the phosphorylation status of SypG is extensive, with at least four hybrid histidine kinases (RscS, SypF, HahK, and BinK) that can affect SypG-dependent transcription of the syp locus.
source: The signaling pathway that controls the phosphorylation status of SypG is extensive, with at least four hybrid histidine kinases (RscS, SypF, HahK, and BinK) that can affect SypG-dependent transcription of the syp locus (Visick et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: RscS is thought to phosphorylate the HPt domain within the C-terminus of SypF, which in turn phosphorylates D53 of SypG.
source: RscS is thought to phosphorylate the HPt domain within the C-terminus of SypF, which in turn phosphorylates D53 of SypG (Norsworthy and Visick, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: BinK is hypothesized to contribute to dephosphorylating SypG.
source: On the other hand, BinK is hypothesized to contribute to dephosphorylating SypG, due to the observation of the ΔbinK mutant exhibiting higher SypG-dependent expression of the syp genes than WT cells (Ludvik et al., 2021).

claim: Increased biofilm production in strains lacking BinK depends on the HPt domain of SypF.
source: Previous work showed that increased biofilm production in strains lacking BinK depends on the HPt domain of SypF (Thompson et al., 2018), which highlights SypF as a potential phospho-donor for SypG in cells harboring a ΔbinK allele.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Elevated LuxO-dependent transcription of Pqrr1 in the ΔbinK mutant is consistent with higher levels of phosphorylated LuxO.
source: Our results that show elevated LuxO-dependent transcription of Pqrr1 in the ΔbinK mutant (Figure 4) are consistent with higher levels of phosphorylated LuxO, which raises the possibility that BinK can dephosphorylate LuxO as well as SypG.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with reference to Figure 4.

claim: BinK can dephosphorylate LuxO as well as SypG.

claim: LuxU accelerates biofilm formation in cells overexpressing SypG.

claim: The ability of LuxO and SypG to each activate transcription of Pqrr1 resembles an OR logic gate that permits gene expression when either one or both of the bEBPs are active.
source: For instance, the ability of LuxO and SypG to each activate transcription of Pqrr1 presented here resembles an OR logic gate that permits gene expression when either one or both of the bEBPs are active (e.g., Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: Molecular OR logic gates have been proposed as important components in engineering therapeutic bacteria that will deliver a drug when certain environmental conditions are satisfied.
source: Molecular OR logic gates have been proposed as important components in engineering therapeutic bacteria that will deliver a drug when certain environmental conditions are satisfied (Brophy and Voigt, 2014).

claim: The σ54-dependent promoters of the syp locus can be activated by SypG but not by LuxO.
source: Despite SypG and LuxO utilizing the overlapping UASs upstream of Pqrr1, it appears that the σ54-dependent promoters of the syp locus can be activated by SypG but not by LuxO (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Determining the mechanism by which the syp promoters are insulated from LuxO in V. fischeri will expand the utility of bEBPs in synthetic biology applications.
source: Consequently, determining the mechanism by which the syp promoters are insulated from LuxO in V. fischeri will not only reveal molecular insight into symbiont biology but will also further expand the utility of bEBPs in synthetic biology applications.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section.
